title: Nonlocality-induced critical-length hierarchy from non-Hermitian competition
authors: Mengjie Yang, Alexander N. Poddubny, Ching Hua Lee
abstract: Spectral transitions in non-Hermitian lattices often arise from the competition between non-reciprocal skin accumulation and inter-component hybridization. In short-range systems formed by two coupled chains, this competition conventionally leads to the logarithmic critical-length law $N_c\sim\ln D$, where $D$ is the transverse separation between the chains. Here we show that long-range hoppings fundamentally reorganizes this critical behavior, producing a hierarchy of distinct scaling laws. When only the hybridization couplings are power-law decaying with exponent $α$, the onset becomes algebraic, $N_c\sim D^{α/3}$. When the hoppings within each chain are themselves also power-law decaying, in addition to the hybridization couplings, the system enters a scale-covariant regime for $α<2$, in which the criticality threshold equation depends only on the system aspect ratio $N_c/D$. At $α=2$ and beyond, this regime is followed by a marginal logarithmically corrected and algebraically corrected regimes, respectively. We identify two new non-local mechanisms that enable this unconventional critical hierarchy: a nonanalytic band-edge dispersion from long-range intra-chain hoppings, and parity-mixing hybridization induced by non-reciprocity. Our results show that nonlocality systematically removes the physical length scales i.e. skin depth underlying conventional critical non-Hermitian skin behavior, offering a platform-independent framework testable in programmable topoelectrical circuits, photonic lattices and digital quantum simulators.
summary: This theoretical work analyzes spectral transitions in coupled non-Hermitian lattices by incorporating long-range hopping interactions. The authors demonstrate that these long-range couplings reorganize the critical behavior from conventional logarithmic scaling to a hierarchy including algebraic and scale-covariant regimes. This offers a generalized framework for understanding stability thresholds in complex quantum systems.
main_problem: The study investigates how long-range hoppings fundamentally reorganize critical spectral behavior in non-Hermitian lattices, moving beyond conventional scaling laws.
main_result: Long-range hoppings induce a hierarchy of distinct critical behaviors, including an algebraic onset and a novel scale-covariant regime, which systematically removes physical length scales like the skin depth.
method: The analysis involves comparing three coupled ladder configurations (Models I, II, III) by analyzing spectral transitions using both finite-size Bloch symbols and time/frequency domain measurements of eigenvalue splitting.
model_or_system: The system models are non-Hermitian lattices formed by two coupled chains exhibiting the Non-Hermitian Skin Effect. The Hamiltonian incorporates nearest-neighbor (NN) and long-range (LR) hopping terms, allowing for three distinct coupling geometries (local/long-range legs and rungs).
key_observables: Critical length scale ($N_c$), spectral transitions (real to complex energy spectra), relative imaginary splitting ($\Delta 	ext{Im}$ or $\Gamma_{\max}$).
important_parameters: Transverse separation ($D$), power-law decay exponent ($\alpha$), and non-reciprocity parameter ($\gamma$).
main_assumptions: The analysis assumes Open Boundary Conditions (OBCs) throughout, and for analytical tractability, the full distance-dependent coupling kernel is sometimes approximated by a constant-kernel form.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate single-chain Bloch spectra and compare $N_c$ vs. $D$ plots for three different nonlocal ladder configurations (Model I, II, III), demonstrating the differing scaling laws.
paper_structure: The paper progresses by defining the physical models (three coupled chains) and then systematically analyzing the critical length scale ($N_c$) associated with spectral transitions using multiple diagnostic tools (Bloch symbols, time/frequency domain measurements). The comparison across different coupling types reveals the hierarchy of scaling laws.
why_interesting: The framework provides a platform-independent understanding of how nonlocality fundamentally alters stability thresholds in open quantum systems, which is highly relevant for designing robust topological or photonic circuits.
